segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Law

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's great novel of fog, law, and the long shadow of secrets.
Bleak House is, by any measure, one of the most ambitious novels in the English language.
It gives us a Court of Chancery that devours lives, a baronet's wife with a buried past, an orphan girl who narrates half the book, and a cast of grotesques and innocents that feels inexhaustible.
Over several episodes, we'll be working through it chapter by chapter — the atmosphere, the characters, the comedy, the tragedy, and the sheer craft of the thing.
Three remarkable guests join me today, and I want to take a moment to introduce them properly.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished literary critics of his generation.

His great insistence is that novels are moral dramas — stories about individual character tested by circumstance — and he has little patience for readings that flatten literature into social programme.
When Dickens gets the psychology right, Edmund will tell us; and when he thinks the sentimentality overwhelms the art, he'll tell us that too.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who has spent his career studying the real institutions behind the literary imagination.
He knows what the Court of Chancery actually was, what poverty actually meant in the 1850s, and he brings that knowledge to bear with a dry wit and a genuine anger about injustice.
If the novel is a piece of evidence about Victorian England, James will tell us what it proves.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has narrated more classic novels for audio than perhaps anyone alive.
He approaches every novel as a performer first — hearing the rhythms, catching the comic timing, knowing which lines were written for the voice and not the page.
Oliver loves the grotesques and the comedy with genuine delight, but he goes very quiet when the novel earns it — and Bleak House earns it more than most.
Today we begin with what Dickens himself gives us first: atmosphere.
The fog, the law, the curse upon the house — and the question of whether Bleak House earns its darkness or simply wallows in it.
One must begin, I think, by acknowledging what Dickens is doing structurally in this novel — which is rather unlike anything he had attempted before.

He divides the narration between two voices: an omniscient narrator of almost biblical authority, and Esther Summerson, who speaks in the first person with characteristic modesty and characteristic unreliability.
The effect is that we are never quite in possession of the whole truth — which is, of course, precisely Dickens's point.
The atmosphere of the novel — the fog, the mud, the perpetual twilight of Chancery — is not merely decorative.
It is the objective correlative of moral obscurity.
And I say that as someone who does not reach for that term lightly.
Edmund is absolutely right about the structural division, and what strikes me — as someone who's had to voice both narrators — is how different the prose actually sounds.
The omniscient narrator is all present tense and cold fury, driving forward like weather.
Esther is all past tense and careful qualification — she is forever apologising for herself.
But she can carry the most extraordinary emotional weight precisely because she underplays.
There is a passage in chapter forty-three where Esther describes the anguish of living near her mother — Lady Dedlock — while being unable to acknowledge her.
She writes:
"Knowing that my mere existence as a living creature was an unforeseen danger in her way, I could not always conquer that terror of myself which had seized me when I first knew the secret."
Terror of herself.
Not of discovery, not of scandal — of her own being.
That is one of the most quietly devastating lines in the whole novel, and it arrives without fanfare in a chapter full of Skimpole's comic nonsense.
Oliver has put his finger on something important there, and I want to pick up on that sense of hidden peril — because it runs through the novel at every level.
There is a passage I find almost unbearably concentrated — the old curse on the Dedlock family, attributed to a crippled ancestral lady.
She has walked the terrace every day, in silence, in worsening pain, saying nothing — and then she falls.
And from the pavement, repulsing her husband as he bends over her, she says:
"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave.
I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
Now, that is gothic machinery — and Dickens knows it is gothic machinery.
But the reason it works is that it is completely credible as the speech of a woman who has been humiliated, who has borne her suffering in silence for years, and who chooses this one moment to speak.
The pride of the house — that phrase lands differently once you've met the present Lady Dedlock and seen what pride has cost her.
James has put it very precisely — and I'd add that the curse functions not as superstition but as structural prophecy within the novel.
Dickens is not asking us to believe in ghosts.
He is asking us to believe that the sins and humiliations of one generation do not dissolve — that they accumulate, that they walk.
The Smallweeds offer the same point in an entirely different register — comic rather than gothic, but equally relentless.
Here is a family that has, over generations, systematically eliminated every trace of childhood from its own children.
The narrator's description of them is one of Dickens's great comic-savage passages.

"Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds."
The word 'gratifying' is doing all the work there — the narrator adopting the Smallweed family's own language to condemn them.
Irony as moral instrument — Johnson would have approved.
Old monkeys with something depressing on their minds — I mean, you cannot improve on that.
And the marvellous thing is that when you meet Grandfather Smallweed in person, Dickens delivers exactly on the promise of that description.
He is simultaneously terrifying and hilarious — which is very hard to do, and Dickens makes it look effortless.
But I want to follow James's thread back to Esther — specifically to the end of chapter fifty-nine, when she arrives at the gate.
This is, to my mind, one of the most technically brilliant passages in all of Dickens — the way he withholds understanding from Esther, and therefore from us.
She sees a woman lying by the iron gate and keeps insisting that this woman was to guide them to her mother.
"She lay there, and they stopped me!
I saw but did not comprehend the solemn and compassionate look in Mr. Woodcourt's face."
She saw but did not comprehend.
Because the woman lying at the gate is her mother — and Dickens makes us know it before Esther does.
That gap between what we know and what she can bear to know — that is where the tragedy lives.
Oliver has described that scene with real precision, and I think it's worth noting what makes it structurally so devastating.
Lady Dedlock has died not in her house, not in her bed, but in the street — at the gate of a paupers' burial ground.
She has, in a very literal sense, walked down the social scale from everything that pride and rank could offer to its absolute opposite.
The curse from chapter seven has been fulfilled — the pride of the house humbled — but in a form far more terrible than any gothic haunting.
That, I think, is what distinguishes Dickens from lesser melodramatists: his punishments are always social as well as personal.
The fog and the law, the curse and the consequence — and we've barely begun.
We'll pick up after the break with the characters at the centre of this world — and the question of whether atmosphere in Bleak House is a device or something altogether more accusatory.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're looking at character under pressure — specifically the way Dickens builds, tests, and in some cases destroys his people.
We have three remarkable readers with us, each bringing a completely different lens to the novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moralist — interested in character tested by circumstance, in goodness and its costs.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — the real institutions behind the fiction, what poverty and law actually meant to the people caught inside them.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic novels than anyone alive — hears Dickens first as a performer, alert to rhythm, timing, and the sheer pleasure of the prose.
Let's begin with character as something constructed from the outside — the way society shapes, flatters, and ultimately controls the people who believe themselves above it all.
Edmund, you've been looking at one of the novel's most quietly devastating passages — Dickens on Lady Dedlock and the machinery of fashion.
Yes, and it is one of those passages that rewards very careful attention, because its comedy conceals something genuinely unsettling.
Dickens gives us Lady Dedlock in all her icy magnificence — and then proceeds to demonstrate, with surgical precision, that she is managed entirely by the people she condescends to.
The passage turns on a beautiful paradox.
She supposes herself inscrutable — and the text shows us that every dim little star revolving about her knows her completely.
The image Dickens reaches for is wonderfully unexpected.
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput"
The great lady and her entire circle — borne off like a toy fleet by people she has never thought to take seriously.
What interests me morally is this: Dickens is not merely satirising snobbery.
He is diagnosing what happens to a character who has entirely abdicated the work of self-knowledge.
That Gulliver image is simply magnificent — and I think it tells us something about how Dickens is writing this passage at the level of pure performance.
He gives voice to the tradespeople directly — Blaze and Sparkle, Sheen and Gloss, the marvellous Mr. Sladdery.
Listen to Sladdery's rhythm — this is written to be spoken aloud.
"you must leave it, if you please, to me, for I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion, sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my finger"
That repeated "sir" — it's obsequious music, and Dickens knows exactly what he's conducting.
The comedy is doing serious work, as Edmund says — but it's also just enormously enjoyable.
The passage is accurate as social history, which makes it even more pointed.
The librarian, the mercer, the jeweller — these were genuinely the gatekeepers of fashionable consumption in mid-Victorian England.
The aristocracy believed they set taste; in practice, taste was manufactured for them and sold back at considerable profit.
What Dickens captures is the complete inversion of the apparent social order — who actually holds the power, and who merely believes they do.
That question — of apparent versus real power — runs through everything Dickens builds around the Dedlocks.

And yet — and this is where I part company slightly from a purely sociological reading — Dickens never lets us forget that Lady Dedlock is also a human being under terrible pressure of her own making.
The satire is genuine, but it is the satire of a moralist, not a pamphleteer.
He is not merely indicting a class — he is showing us the spiritual cost of choosing performance over authenticity.
Which brings us, in a way, to a very different kind of character entirely — Boythorn.
Boythorn — now there is a man who has chosen authenticity with perhaps excessive commitment.
Every reader who has encountered this passage will remember it — because it is written at full throttle from first word to last.
The escalating dispute with Sir Leicester — fire engines, man traps, split peas — it's an aria of magnificent indignation.
But what makes it work is the rhythm of the final beat.
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
That laughter isn't decorative — it's the whole point of the man.
He is not embittered by this feud — he is nourished by it.
The legal detail is precise — and darkly funny, if you know anything about mid-Victorian property disputes.
Rights of way over private land were genuinely contested in this period — they were class battles conducted through writs and counter-writs.
What Boythorn understands — and what makes him so enjoyable — is that the process itself has become the point.
He and Sir Leicester have both lost sight of the pathway itself and are now simply conducting an operatic argument about who they are.
Which is, of course, exactly what Jarndyce and Jarndyce does to everyone it touches — and that's the novel's deeper current running beneath the comedy.
That connection is essential — and it brings us to the novel's most painful portrait of a young man caught in exactly that current.
Richard Carstone.
What I find most moving in Jarndyce's address to Richard and Ada is its combination of warmth and warning — and the exquisite sadness of that repeated phrase.
He speaks of having contemplated their union — their future together — but insists on the distance at which he held the thought.

"I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together. But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
That "afar off" — spoken three times — is Jarndyce telling Richard, in the gentlest possible way, that the preconditions for happiness must be built before they can be claimed.
Richard, of course, cannot hear it.
The parenthesis to Ada — "don't be shy, my dear" — is a tiny gem of characterisation buried inside the gravity of the speech.
Jarndyce never loses his tenderness even when he is delivering the most searching of counsels.
And as Edmund says — Richard cannot hear it.
The whole tragedy of Richard is that he is surrounded by people who love him and speak plainly to him — and he hears only what the suit whispers.
Dickens is very precise about that — it is a kind of possession.
Richard's situation had real-world parallels that any reader in 1853 would have recognised instantly.
Chancery suits of this kind could last decades — there were families who had staked everything on a judgment that never came.
The deferred hope was the mechanism — it kept people paralysed, unable to begin their actual lives.
Jarndyce's warning — "afar off, Rick, afar off" — is also, if you read it carefully, a warning about the suit itself.
Begin your life now, with what you have.
Richard, fatally, cannot.
Against that portrait of paralysis, Dickens places a vision of something almost unbearably opposite — children who have no choice but to act, because no one else will.
The passage in which Esther opens the door on Charley Neckett's younger siblings is, to my mind, among the most quietly devastating in the novel.
Dickens does not editorialise.
He simply describes what Esther sees.
"In a poor room with a sloping ceiling and containing very little furniture was a mite of a boy, some five or six years old, nursing and hushing a heavy child of eighteen months."
"There was no fire, though the weather was cold; both children were wrapped in some poor shawls and tippets as a substitute."
A substitute for a fire.
The word does more moral work than a paragraph of indignation could.
I've read that passage aloud more than once in public, and I can tell you — the room goes very still.
It's the boy walking up and down that does it — he's not sitting there waiting to be rescued, he is doing the work.
He is nursing and hushing, with the baby's head on his shoulder.
A child of five or six.
Dickens earned that silence — he doesn't ask for it, he simply places the image in front of you and trusts the reader.
The social reality behind that image was entirely commonplace in the 1850s.
When a parent died or was incapacitated, the older children simply became the caregivers — there was no other provision.
Dickens knew this world intimately — and he knew that what shocked his readers about such scenes was not their rarity but their absolute ordinariness.
This is happening right now, the novel says — not in some Gothic past, not in a fairytale poverty.
In a room with a sloping ceiling, in the cold.
And then Dickens brings us, finally, to a moment of pure counterweight — one of the most tender gestures in the entire novel.
Esther is led out of the porch of a new house by Jarndyce.
And Dickens gives us the moment in nine words.
"We went out of the porch and he showed me written over it, Bleak House."
The same name — the same bleak name — given now as a gift, as a home.
Dickens understood that the meaning of a word can be entirely transformed by the love attached to it.
Nine words — and the entire novel earns them.
Every preceding image of bleakness — the fog, the court, the cold room, the children in the shawls — all of it is gathered into those nine words and reversed.
That's the craft of the novel at its most formidable — the architecture working across hundreds of pages to make one small sentence feel enormous.
It's also, I think, a quietly political act on Dickens's part.
He takes the novel's title — its most relentless signifier of decay and despair — and hands it to Esther as something salvaged, renewed.
It suggests that even the most blighted institutions, the most broken circumstances, are not entirely beyond the reach of human care and agency.
That is not naïve optimism — it is something harder and more durable than that.
Character under pressure — and character as the one thing that pressure cannot ultimately destroy.
Thank you, Edmund, James, and Oliver — we'll continue in our next segment with the novel's great institutions, and what they do to the people inside them.

segments.title: The Performance of Conscience: Reading Dickens's Rhythms

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been following Dickens through the fog of Chancery, through Chesney Wold, through the lodging houses of Tom-All-Alone's.
Today we turn to something that lives underneath all of that: the rhythms of the prose itself.
How Dickens writes, not just what he writes — the timing, the voice, the shock hidden inside the sentence.
Our guide for this segment is Oliver Trevelyan — actor, audiobook narrator, and the man who has probably read more Dickens aloud than anyone living.
We're also joined, as ever, by Sir Edmund Leigh and Professor James Blackstone.
Oliver, let's start with you — because this is, in a sense, your territory.
When you sit down to narrate Bleak House, what do you hear first?
What I hear first is the punctuation.
Dickens doesn't punctuate for grammar — he punctuates for breath, for timing, for the exact moment the reader needs to feel the blow land.
There's a passage early on — the old woman in Chancery court, the one who was herself a ward.
She says something that could have been a speech, a lament, a long paragraph of grief.
Instead Dickens strips it to the bone.
Listen to this:
"Neither of the three served or saved me. I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment."
Every full stop is a door closing.
Youth. Hope. Beauty. Judgment. The Day of Judgment. The sentences get shorter as the stakes get higher.
That is not grammar. That is a performance score.
I think that's exactly right, and it points to something one rarely hears said plainly enough about Dickens.
He is a moral writer, yes — but his morality is expressed through form, not through lecture.
That old woman's speech is devastating precisely because it is so bare.
There is no authorial intrusion, no narrator weeping on her behalf.
The character simply speaks, in that extraordinary staccato, and the form carries the indictment entirely.
Johnson said that the business of the poet is to examine not the individual but the species.
That woman is not merely a mad ward of Chancery — she is the species of all those destroyed by institutions that outlive their purpose.
And Dickens knows, I think, that comedy and tragedy can share the same sentence.
He gives us the old Smallweed grandfather — one of the most grotesque comic characters in all of English fiction.
And he puts the most violent insults imaginable inside what is essentially an obituary notice for Bart's father.
The passage is structured so that every time old Smallweed reaches a point of genuine pathos, he explodes at his wife.
Here — I cannot resist reading this one in full:

"just as he was beginning to build up the house that he had been making the foundations for, through many a year — you jade of a magpie, jackdaw, and poll-parrot, what do you mean! — he took ill and died of a low fever"
The whole life of a man — ambition, years of effort, death — inserted inside an insult like a letter inside an envelope.
That is not an accident of style. That is a miniaturist working at the absolute height of his powers.
The Smallweed household is, amongst other things, a scrupulously accurate portrait of a certain kind of Victorian money-lending operation.
But what Dickens understands — and this is the thing that separates him from the social reformers of his day — is that greed deforms people into comedy.
Old Smallweed is not presented as a villain to be condemned in a pamphlet. He is presented as a spectacle to be witnessed, and that is far more damning.
What Oliver's reading catches — and I think this matters enormously — is that the comedy doesn't let us off.
We laugh, yes. But the laughter sticks in the throat when we register what's inside the envelope, as he put it.
And then Dickens can shift registers entirely — can move, within the same chapter, to something almost cinematic in its shock.
There is a moment in chapter forty-one that I consider one of the great single sentences in the novel.
Tulkinghorn is pacing on the leads above his chambers — perfectly composed, utterly in command as always.
And then, through a glass door, two eyes meet his own.
"The blood has not flushed into his face so suddenly and redly for many a long year as when he recognizes Lady Dedlock."
The word "redly" — it's almost brutal in its physicality.
Dickens strips the iron composure off Tulkinghorn in nine words, and we feel it like a slap.
That sentence is a reminder that Dickens's prose, at its finest, is not decorative — it is diagnostic.
Tulkinghorn has been constructed throughout the novel as a man of absolute self-containment.
He is the novel's most frightening figure precisely because he feels nothing — or appears to.
So when the blood rushes to his face, we understand in an instant the full architecture of his secret power over Lady Dedlock.
One sentence does what pages of exposition could not.
I want to bring in Vholes for a moment — because Vholes is where Dickens's comic and satirical voices fuse into something almost sinister.
He is a lawyer, and everything he says is technically polite and professionally defensible.
And yet the cumulative effect of his speech is deeply wrong — there is something vampiric about the courtesy.
He is assessing Ada's eligibility as a match for Richard — and he does so by outsourcing even his aesthetic judgment to the clerks of the Inn.
"I dare say the young lady is equally eligible in that point of view. She is considered so (I have heard) among the clerks in the Inn, and it is a point more in their way than in mine."
The phrase "in their way than in mine" is doing enormous work.
It suggests that beauty is a form of currency he cannot be bothered to exchange — that human feeling is simply outside his professional jurisdiction.
Narrating Vholes is a particular pleasure — and a particular challenge.
Because the voice must be utterly flat. No irony in the delivery — the irony is entirely Dickens's, and you must trust it completely.
The moment you nudge the performance — put even a hint of a smirk in — you destroy the effect.
And then there's Mr. Bucket — who is the opposite of Vholes in almost every way.
Bucket performs warmth as a professional instrument. He is endlessly, relentlessly genial — and it is terrifying.
He corners Smallweed with this extraordinary conversational air — stooping over him, absolutely cordial.
"And so you chance to find, you know, a paper with the signature of Jarndyce to it. Don't you?"
"Don't you?" — delivered with perfect cheerfulness — is as close to a hand around the throat as language gets.
Dickens built a detective before detective fiction existed, and he built him entirely out of social warmth weaponised.
Oliver puts his finger on something I think is absolutely central to Dickens's genius.
His characters perform — they perform their social roles, their professional masks, their moral claims — and he lets the performance reveal the soul.
Bucket's geniality, Vholes's professional discretion, old Smallweed's financial piety — these are all performances.
And the prose rhythm is the means by which Dickens makes us see through them — or sometimes, crucially, fail to.
That word — performance — feels like exactly the right note to carry forward.
The idea that the prose itself is a kind of stage direction, written for a reader who listens.
We'll be back shortly to look at how Bleak House handles its great institutional villain — Chancery itself — and what the novel makes of the people ground up inside it.

segments.title: A Woman's Ruin: Lady Dedlock's Secret Exposed

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've reached one of the novel's most electrically charged territories — the slow, terrible exposure of Lady Dedlock's secret.
And with me today are three voices I couldn't be more pleased to have around this table.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, moral critic of the first order, and a man whose patience with slovenly reading is, shall we say, limited.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who reminds us that every document in this novel had real teeth.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, audiobook narrator without equal — who hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.
The segment we're exploring turns on a single devastating sentence delivered — with perfect indirection — by Mr. Tulkinghorn.
Sir Leicester reads it aloud from a letter, entirely without comprehension, to the one person in the room it will destroy.
That scene is one of the great pieces of comic-gothic timing in the whole novel.
Sir Leicester fumbling with his eyeglass, losing his place, apologising — all while Lady Dedlock sits and waits for the blow to land.
And the message itself, when it finally comes, is so measured, so lawyerly in its courtesy.
'I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him.'
Three words at the end. 'I have seen him.' The ground shifts under everything.
And Sir Leicester hasn't the faintest idea what he's just read aloud to his wife.
What strikes me most about that passage is the structural irony Dickens builds into Sir Leicester's very incomprehension.
His obliviousness is not stupidity — it is the blindness of a man whose world has been arranged so that certain things simply cannot be true.
His class, his dignity, his absolute trust in the Dedlock name — these are not vanity.
They are the architecture of his moral universe, and Dickens knows how much it will cost to demolish them.
Tulkinghorn, by contrast, arrives at Chesney Wold with the unhurried deliberateness of a man who knows exactly the weight he carries.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary portrait of him approaching across the terrace.
'He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.'
Every crease of his dress. The man is practically a filing cabinet with a waistcoat.
That image is more than atmospheric — it's forensically accurate.
A solicitor of Tulkinghorn's kind would in practice hold extraordinary power over aristocratic families, precisely because he knew where every skeleton was kept.
He wasn't a servant, but he wasn't an equal either — he existed in a space of calculated ambiguity that gave him enormous leverage.
And Dickens captures this perfectly — 'Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret.'
We simply do not know what Tulkinghorn wants. Power? Security? Something like revenge on the class he serves?
The novel never fully answers that, and neither did the legal system — solicitors held information as currency in ways the courts never quite managed to regulate.
And then comes the scene I never tire of performing — the two of them in the room together, watched by Sir Leicester who understands nothing of what he's watching.
'Sir Leicester has looked at the fire, with the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.'
That line! The ancestral portrait come to life — or rather, come to non-life.
He has been reduced to a decorative object in the scene that will eventually ruin him.
Meanwhile Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn are locked in something almost like armed surveillance.
Dickens keeps doubling back on himself with this extraordinary anaphora — 'whether each... whether each... what each would give to know.'
It becomes almost ritualistic, a kind of legal litany of mutual suspicion.
The phrase 'hidden, for the time, in their own hearts' deserves more attention than it usually receives.
'For the time' — that tiny qualification carries the weight of a tragedy.
Dickens is telling us — with the calm authority of an omniscient narrator — that this concealment is temporary.
The prose performs the very act of surveillance it describes — it watches Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn even as they watch each other.
The full passage is quite remarkable in its sustained tension.
'Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.'
'Exhausted deity.' Two words for a woman performing a social role that has utterly consumed her.
What we should not lose sight of is what is actually being concealed — and what it meant in law and society.
Lady Dedlock had a child before her marriage — a child she believed dead — and she has built an entire life on suppressing that fact.
The information Mr. Jarndyce eventually discloses to Esther came originally from a woman who went to extraordinary lengths to remain unknown.
He tells Esther: 'That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never for any human consideration disclose.'
'For any human consideration.' That is not the language of shame alone — that is the language of absolute terror.
In mid-Victorian England, an illegitimate child and a pre-marital liaison could destroy a woman utterly — and the law provided her no protection whatsoever.
Tulkinghorn knows this. That is his power.
And yet — and this is what I find most moving — Lady Dedlock never breaks.
Not in these scenes. Her insolent grace — that extraordinary phrase — is her armour and her performance simultaneously.
When she passes Tulkinghorn in that doorway — 'with her usual fatigued manner and insolent grace' — it's almost a duel.
She is on the edge of an abyss and she walks past him as though he is a hat-stand.
That takes a kind of courage — or a kind of despair so complete it looks like courage.
Oliver puts his finger on the moral complexity that elevates Lady Dedlock above a merely cautionary figure.
Dickens is not content to make her simply a fallen woman awaiting punishment.
She has dignity, she has intelligence, and she has — I think — genuine love for the child she has never been permitted to acknowledge.
Her suffering is not presented as just deserts — it is presented as tragedy in the classical sense.
A noble character brought low not entirely by her own fault, but by circumstance, by a remorseless antagonist, and by the brutal arithmetic of a society that cannot forgive her.
That tension between guilt and tragedy, between personal failing and social cruelty, lies at the very heart of what this novel does.
And the instrument of Lady Dedlock's exposure — Tulkinghorn, that speechless repository of noble confidences — is himself one of Dickens's most elusive creations.
We'll continue to follow that thread — and the trail it leaves toward ruin — as our discussion unfolds.

segments.title: The Boy Nobody Wanted: Jo and Social Abandonment

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great sprawling masterpiece apart — chapter by chapter, voice by voice, argument by argument.
I'm your host, and today we're gathering around one of the novel's most devastating creations: Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
A boy with no surname, no schooling, no one in the world — and yet a moral presence that haunts the entire novel.
To think through what Dickens is doing with Jo — and what he's doing to us — I'm joined by three brilliant minds.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and the most courteous defender of the moral imagination in English letters.
He reads Dickens as a novelist of character and conscience, not as a social pamphleteer.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what the institutions Dickens depicts actually did to real people — and he doesn't let us forget it.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone alive — reads Dickens the way Dickens wanted to be read: aloud, with full relish.
Let's begin with the inquest in Chapter Eleven — the moment Jo is called to testify, and Dickens strips the boy's situation down to its unbearable essentials.
There's a moment in that inquest passage that I've read aloud more times than I can count, and it never, ever loses its force.
Dickens gives us the coroner's questions rendered in free indirect style — and the answers are devastating in their plainness.
Listen to what the text actually says:
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Five words. Then four. And the whole world is contained in them.
Dickens doesn't say 'the destitute orphan' or 'the friendless waif' — he gives us the inventory, in Jo's own rhythm, and leaves the rest to silence.
And then — only then — does he ask: what's home?
What strikes me, and I think it is the crucial point, is that Dickens does not make Jo pitiable by making him passive.
The boy has moral knowledge. He knows a broom is a broom, and he knows it is wicked to tell a lie.
Dickens is at pains to tell us, in the very passage Oliver has just read:
"Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie. Don't recollect who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both."
Here is a soul that has received no formal instruction yet has arrived at the rudiments of honest character entirely on its own.
That is not social critique. That is Dickens's oldest and deepest belief: that moral sense is innate, not the property of education or rank.
Jo is, in that sense, a rebuke not to any particular institution but to anyone who has squandered the moral instinct he was born with.
I take Edmund's point about innate moral sense, but I want to press on what society does with that moral sense once it has identified it.
The coroner's inquest won't take Jo's oath, because he has no understanding of what an oath means in the eyes of the law.
He is, in every legal sense, a non-person.
And yet consider the system that produced this non-person.
In the same chapters, Jarndyce gives us the definitive portrait of how Chancery works — and I use the word 'works' with the deepest irony.
He calls it — and this is Dickens at his most finely satirical —
"the whole thing will be vastly ceremonious, wordy, unsatisfactory, and expensive, and I call it, in general, Wiglomeration."
The resources consumed in that machine — the fees, the delays, the ritual expense — are precisely the resources that never reach a boy like Jo.
Wiglomeration — it is one of the great comic coinages in the English novel, and yet it does the most serious work.
Jarndyce spits it out as if just inventing the word were a form of relief from the unbearable absurdity of the thing itself.
And Dickens being Dickens, he needs a counter-image to set against all that legal fog and expenditure.
Which is why the description of Bleak House itself — the actual house — is so carefully, almost tenderly constructed.
Esther sums it up with one of those long, accumulating Dickensian sentences that you have to trust — you just have to let it carry you:
"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw"
That warmth is not ironic. It's completely real — and it makes the world Jo inhabits feel all the colder by contrast.
Oliver has touched on something I want to linger on: that warmth is not merely decorative.
Bleak House — the house, not the case — is itself a moral argument.
Jarndyce has created a home that offers exactly what the Chancery system cannot: order without rigidity, comfort without ostentation, welcome without condition.
And the furniture — old-fashioned rather than old, as Esther notes — agrees in nothing but, and this is the key phrase, their perfect neatness.
That is a domestic ideal that Dickens sets against the chaos of the court — not as polemic, but as a counter-vision of how human beings might choose to treat one another.
I don't disagree with that reading, but I think we have to ask who is excluded from that warmth.
When Mrs. Piper is called at the inquest, the testimony she gives about the dead man Nemo — and about Jo — is a remarkable document of how the poor are perceived by their neighbours.
The prose mimics her syntax — breathless, digressive, unpunctuated — and the effect is comic, but the content is bleak.
The key detail, delivered almost in passing:
"the plaintive — so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased — was reported to have sold himself."
She cannot even name him correctly — 'plaintiff' mangled to 'plaintive' — and yet she has the confidence to report that he sold his soul.
The rumour mill of the urban poor, grinding reputations to dust — that is as real an institution as Chancery, and just as destructive.
The comedy of Mrs. Piper is almost cruel in its precision — and Dickens absolutely intends that discomfort.
She has seen the plaintive 'wexed and worrited by the children' — notice, the children are tormenting him, not the other way around.
And the one exception, the one relationship Nemo had with any living soul, is Jo — 'the boy that sweeps the crossing down the lane over the way round the corner.'
That string of prepositions is the geography of total marginality — so far to the edge of things that the directions themselves start to dissolve.
And here is where I want to bring in Vholes and Kenge — because the system that ignores Jo is the same system that protects itself with elaborate courtesy.
When reform is suggested, when someone proposes changing the laws that feed the Wiglomeration, the answer is always the same.
Kenge invokes Vholes — that grimly respectable solicitor — as a shield against all change:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
Said as if it were an unanswerable argument. And before Parliamentary committees, for ten years, it was.
The respectability of Mr. Vholes is worth more, to the system, than the testimony of a thousand Jos.
That is Dickens's satirical genius at full stretch, and I will not argue with it.
But I would note that the instrument of that satire is still an individual — Kenge, Vholes — making a choice, however self-serving, however venal.
Dickens does not let the system off the hook by making it abstract.
The system has faces, names, voices — and consequently, moral responsibility.
A system with faces — and a boy with no name beyond Jo.
That tension — between the machinery of law and the singularity of a human being — sits at the heart of Bleak House, and I suspect it will stay with us through the rest of this episode.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan for a conversation that has, I think, done justice to one of the most quietly devastating passages Dickens ever wrote.
We'll be back shortly to follow the fog wherever it leads next.

segments.title: Invention and Order: How Dickens Shapes Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of the greatest novels in the English language and opens it room by room.
I'm your host, and today we're asking a question that sits at the very heart of this novel: how does Dickens actually shape Bleak House?
Not just what he puts in, but how the architecture works — the structure of feeling, the moral geometry, the way invention and order hold each other in tension.
To help us think through it, I'm joined by three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose deep conviction is that great fiction is, above all, a moral art — and that reading Bleak House as sociology is to miss its living heart.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real world into the room — the courts, the poverty, the institutional machinery that Dickens is anatomising.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels for the ear than almost anyone alive — he reads Dickens as a performer first, hearing the rhythms that the page alone cannot fully carry.
Gentlemen, let's begin with the question of how Dickens constructs his characters — not as types, but as moral beings whose fates accumulate meaning.
Edmund, the passages you've been looking at this week seem to circle a particular quality — a kind of prophetic tenderness in the way Dickens plants detail.
Thank you.
What strikes me most forcefully about these passages, taken together, is how Dickens engineers what I can only call retrospective illumination.
He plants an object, or a gesture, or a phrase, which appears at first to carry only its immediate weight — tenderness, pity, the ordinary texture of feeling.
And then, chapters and volumes later, that same object returns and the reader understands, with something approaching dread, exactly what it has been carrying all along.
The supreme instance, to my mind, is the handkerchief passage in chapter eight.
Esther raises a handkerchief to look at a sleeping baby in a brickmaker's cottage, and the prose does something quietly extraordinary.
She writes:

"How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the child through Ada's drooping hair as her pity bent her head—how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!"
The halo around the child — that is the detail Dickens has placed like a seed.
The reader feels the beauty first.
Only later do we understand that the handkerchief, the emblem of one woman's compassion, will travel to another woman's grief — to Lady Dedlock's dead body.
That is not sociology, that is not social programme — that is the moral imagination of a master novelist working at the very peak of his art.
Edmund, you've gone straight to the heart of it — and as a reader, I can tell you that passage is one of the most technically difficult in the novel to perform.
Because Esther is telling us, from her future vantage point, what her past self did not know.
The phrase "how little I thought" is not merely rhetorical — it is Esther's own retrospective sorrow entering the sentence.
When you read it aloud, you have to hold those two tenses in the voice simultaneously — the innocence of the moment, and the knowledge that has since broken over it.
And then that ending — the woman at the door, saying in her old soothing manner, "Jenny, Jenny!"
"Jenny, Jenny!"
It's three syllables, repeated, and Dickens has somehow put an entire relationship into them — grief, habit, love, helplessness.
That is the novelist as composer.
I take the point about moral imagination, and I won't quarrel with it.
But I'd observe that what makes that passage devastating is also its social precision.
Jenny and her companion are brickmakers' wives — women living in genuine squalor, legally invisible, unprotected by any institution in the novel.
The tenderness of that scene is inseparable from the fact that these women have nothing.
And the handkerchief — an object belonging to Esther, a woman of some station — passing through that world is also a passage between social worlds.
Dickens is a moralist, certainly — Edmund is right about that.
But his moral imagination is always embedded in a specific, documented, socially located world.
You can't separate the two — and frankly I think the attempt to do so diminishes both.
I accept the amendment, James — though I'd say it slightly differently.
What Dickens shows us, at his most searching, is that certain virtues transcend the social position in which they happen to be lodged.
Consider what the omniscient narrator says of Sir Leicester Dedlock in chapter fifty-eight.
This is a man who has every reason — by his own lights — to feel betrayed and humiliated.
And yet the prose says this:
"His noble earnestness, his fidelity, his gallant shielding of her, his generous conquest of his own wrong and his own pride for her sake, are simply honourable, manly, and true."
And then the sentence that follows — which is the moral centre of this whole novel as far as I'm concerned:
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
Children of the dust — that is Burke and the Bible and the English moral tradition all at once.
Dickens is not dissolving class — he is saying that genuine virtue renders it irrelevant, momentarily, in the light of something larger.
The rhythm of that sentence is quite remarkable, you know — "both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
Three parallel clauses, each one gaining weight, and the third landing on "shine equally" — which is almost a benediction.
Dickens learned from the Authorised Version, and you can hear it.
But what I find equally wonderful is the scene just before it — Sir Leicester making his formal declaration before witnesses.
Here is a man half-paralysed by a stroke, and he insists on arranging everything with the full ceremony of his class and his name.
He says — and you have to hear the full weight of this:

"I desire to say in your presence—and in the presence of my old retainer and friend, Mrs. Rouncewell, whose truth and fidelity no one can question, and in the presence of her son George, who comes back like a familiar recollection of my youth in the home of my ancestors at Chesney Wold—in case I should relapse, in case I should not recover."
That accumulation of clauses — the rolling in of witnesses, the naming of the house, the repeated "in case" — is a man making his will with the last of his dignity.
It's heartbreaking, and it's also, in a very precise way, funny — because Dickens understands that pomposity and genuine feeling are not mutually exclusive.
That coexistence of the comic and the genuinely pathetic is, I'd argue, where Dickens is most distinctively himself.
And it operates at the level of the institution as much as the individual character.
Look at what he does with Vholes — the solicitor who attends Richard Carstone through the final stages of the Chancery suit.
Vholes is a legal grotesque, certainly — but Dickens makes him something stranger and more disturbing than mere villainy.
He gives Esther, and through her the reader, this extraordinary speech in chapter sixty:
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account."
And then:
"I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one."
"Though it can be charged to no one" — that phrase, in context, is devastating.
Vholes is the perfect embodiment of an institution that destroys people while scrupulously observing every form.
He cannot be prosecuted, he cannot be shamed, he cannot be exposed — because everything he does is, in the technical sense, lawful.
That is what made Chancery so appalling in practice — and Dickens understood it with the precision of someone who had worked in a law office as a young man.
I would not contest a word of that.
Though I'd observe that Vholes also functions as something beyond a critique of the legal system.
He is a study in a particular moral failure — the abdication of personal responsibility behind professional form.
And then, within the same chapter, Dickens pivots — because Ada's devotion to Richard is set in direct moral contrast.
In chapter fifty-one, when Ada comes to Richard in his final decline, the narrator gives us a moment of almost wordless beauty.
Esther writes:
"my darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me."
"Oh, what a loving and devoted face I saw!"
Vholes discharges duty; Ada performs love.
That is the moral architecture of Bleak House — Dickens sets them in the same world, the same chapter, and asks the reader to feel the difference in the bone.
That image of Ada's golden hair falling like sunlight is one that stays with me every time I read it.
Esther's narration is often self-effacing to the point where modern readers find her trying.
But in this moment she doesn't describe herself at all — she just turns the full light of her attention on Ada.
And that act of selfless witness is, quietly, the most Esther-like thing she could do.
Dickens has constructed a narrator whose very mode of seeing is her moral character.
You can't separate how she looks at the world from who she is.
That connection between character and perception — between who Esther is and how she sees — feels like one of the deepest structural innovations in the novel.
And it's something we'll be returning to.
But for now, I want to hold the image Edmund gave us — of Vholes and Ada, side by side, as the two poles of this novel's moral world.
Form without love, and love without form — Bleak House asks which of those can sustain a human life.
We'll be back after the break to follow that question further.

segments.title: Closing: The Moral Imagination of Bleak House

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through the fog and the courts and the great, teeming world of Bleak House.
And I want to close by asking each of you — what is the moral imagination at the heart of this novel?
Not the satire, not the fog — but what Dickens believes about how human beings ought to live and love and persist.
The answer, I think, is given to us directly by John Jarndyce — and given with extraordinary plainness, which is itself instructive.
This is a novelist who trusts his readers enough to say what he means through a character rather than hiding it in atmosphere.
Jarndyce speaks to Richard, and what he says is this:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
That is the novel's moral centre in two sentences.
Not Providence alone — that would be quietism. Not effort alone — that would be mere Victorian self-help.
The two together. That is what Burke would call a disposition — a formed habit of the whole character.
Edmund is right to start there, and I want to add the institutional dimension — because Richard's failure is not merely personal.
There is a moment where Mrs. Badger — of all people — delivers a quietly devastating clinical verdict on the young man.
She tells Esther, in perfectly measured terms:

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
The contrast with Woodcourt is precise and deliberate.
Vocation — real vocation — is what the novel asks of its young men, and what the Chancery world systematically destroys.
Richard cannot commit to medicine because a part of him has already been surrendered to Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
And yet, for all that darkness, what Dickens gives us in these passages is extraordinarily tender.
There's a scene where Esther sits between Ada and Richard — one on each side — and the three of them talk through the night about what love actually demands.
Esther tells us, with that characteristic blend of delight and sobriety:
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself — and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were."
That parenthesis — 'I enjoyed it too much myself' — is pure Dickens.
He won't let the moral lesson arrive without the warmth. He earns the gravity with the pleasure first.
And Jarndyce himself earns something quite remarkable in the way he handles these young people.
He does not moralize by withholding — he moralize by trusting.
He says to them — and this is the great Jarndyce speech in miniature:

"If you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
'Nothing monstrous or uncommon.' That is a man who understands human nature without contempt for it.
That is the moral imagination I would defend against any merely political reading of this novel.
I won't quarrel with Edmund's Jarndyce — he's right, it's a magnificent passage.
But I'd note that Jarndyce's wisdom is inseparable from the world that has failed Richard.
When he tells Richard, 'if you entertain the supposition that any real success ever was wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here' — that is not just personal counsel.
That is a diagnosis of what Chancery does to its victims — it sells them the fantasy of sudden, unearned resolution.
The moral and the institutional are not separable in this novel. That is what makes it great.
The last image Esther gives us in this chapter — and I find it extraordinary — is purely visual.
Ada and Richard walk away through a sunlit room, and Esther watches them go.
Listen to how she renders it:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
You can't perform that without pausing. You simply stop and let it be.
The whole novel's foreshadowing compressed into a shift in the weather. Dickens at his most devastating.
I can think of no finer place to close than that image — the sun clouding over as they go.
Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, Oliver Trevelyan — thank you for everything you have brought to this conversation today.
The moral imagination of Bleak House — the compassion, the institutional fury, the tenderness toward ordinary human frailty — all of it held together in one extraordinary novel.
For Bleak House Unpacked, thank you for listening.

c43:p0.text:
It matters little now how much I thought of my living mother who had
told me evermore to consider her dead. I could not venture to
approach her or to communicate with her in writing, for my sense of
the peril in which her life was passed was only to be equalled by my
fears of increasing it. Knowing that my mere existence as a living
creature was an unforeseen danger in her way, I could not always
conquer that terror of myself which had seized me when I first knew
the secret. At no time did I dare to utter her name. I felt as if I
did not even dare to hear it. If the conversation anywhere, when I
was present, took that direction, as it sometimes naturally did, I
tried not to hear: I mentally counted, repeated something that I
knew, or went out of the room. I am conscious now that I often did
these things when there can have been no danger of her being spoken
of, but I did them in the dread I had of hearing anything that might
lead to her betrayal, and to her betrayal through me.
c43:p0.summary: Esther describes the anguish of living in proximity to her mother while maintaining absolute distance, unable even to speak her name or hear it mentioned without psychological distress.
c43:p0.best_quote: Knowing that my mere existence as a living creature was an unforeseen danger in her way, I could not always conquer that terror of myself which had seized me when I first knew the secret.

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.
c7:p59.best_quote: I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!

c21:p4.text:
His spirit shone through his son, to whom he had always preached of
“going out” early in life and whom he made a clerk in a sharp
scrivener’s office at twelve years old. There the young gentleman
improved his mind, which was of a lean and anxious character, and
developing the family gifts, gradually elevated himself into the
discounting profession. Going out early in life and marrying late, as
his father had done before him, he too begat a lean and
anxious-minded son, who in his turn, going out early in life and
marrying late, became the father of Bartholomew and Judith Smallweed,
twins. During the whole time consumed in the slow growth of this
family tree, the house of Smallweed, always early to go out and late
to marry, has strengthened itself in its practical character, has
discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books,
fairy-tales, fictions, and fables, and banished all levities
whatsoever. Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born
to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced
have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something
depressing on their minds.
c21:p4.summary: The narrator traces how successive Smallweed generations have perpetuated a culture of early entry into commerce and late marriage, deliberately eliminating all levity and amusement, producing stunted premature adults.
c21:p4.best_quote: Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds.

I could repeat this in my mind too, but I had not the least idea what
it meant. I saw before me, lying on the step, the mother of the dead
child. She lay there with one arm creeping round a bar of the iron
gate and seeming to embrace it. She lay there, who had so lately
spoken to my mother. She lay there, a distressed, unsheltered,
senseless creature. She who had brought my mother’s letter, who could
give me the only clue to where my mother was; she, who was to guide
us to rescue and save her whom we had sought so far, who had come to
this condition by some means connected with my mother that I could
not follow, and might be passing beyond our reach and help at that
moment; she lay there, and they stopped me! I saw but did not
comprehend the solemn and compassionate look in Mr. Woodcourt’s face.
I saw but did not comprehend his touching the other on the breast to
keep him back. I saw him stand uncovered in the bitter air, with a
reverence for something. But my understanding for all this was gone.
c59:p107.summary: Esther realizes that the woman lying at the gate—who brought her mother's letter, who was to guide them to her—is her mother herself, dead, and she cannot understand why Woodcourt and Bucket have stopped her.

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput

c9:p49.text:
“By my soul,” exclaimed Mr. Boythorn, suddenly firing another volley,
“that fellow is, and his father was, and his grandfather was, the
most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by
some inexplicable mistake of Nature, born in any station of life but
a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should
not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and
living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the
existence of those lurking ruffians. He brings actions for trespass;
I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and
battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha,
ha!”
c9:p49.summary: Boythorn launches an elaborate account of his escalating disputes with Sir Leicester over a right of way, detailing the volleys of letters, his theatrical retaliation with a fire engine, his destruction of gates, and the counter-actions in law, all recounted with relish and concluding with triumphant laughter.
c9:p49.best_quote: He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!

“Rick,” said Mr. Jarndyce, “I am glad to have won your confidence. I
hope to preserve it. When I contemplated these relations between us

The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.

you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”
c13:p118.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.
c13:p118.best_quote: Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it.

“My dear Miss Summerson,” she replied, “on Mr. Carstone’s character
and conduct. He is of such a very easy disposition that probably he
would never think it worth while to mention how he really feels, but
he feels languid about the profession. He has not that positive
interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided
impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a
tiresome pursuit. Now, this is not promising. Young men like Mr.
Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can
do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a
very little money and through years of considerable endurance and
disappointment. But I am quite convinced that this would never be the
case with Mr. Carstone.”

c13:p99.text:
There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.
c13:p99.summary: Richard and Ada confide to Esther their mutual love, placing themselves on either side of her. Esther counsels them about the demands of enduring love and promises to speak to Mr. Jarndyce.

c13:p115.text:
“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”
c13:p115.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.

c13:p124.text:
The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up
in his face, listening, and seemed to see nothing else. So young, so
beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through
the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the
years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed
away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that
had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun
was clouded over.
c13:p124.summary: As Ada and Richard leave, Esther observes them passing through sunlit rooms, young and full of hope, but the sun clouds over as they depart, suggesting a foreboding shadow.
